body_md: Every value has one **owner**. When owner goes out of scope, value is dropped. No GC, no manual free. This single rule eliminates double-free and leaks by construction.
hook: Rust has no garbage collector — yet memory frees itself perfectly.

quiz.explain: Owner going out of scope triggers automatic drop.
quiz.q: When is a String freed?

takeaway: Scope exit drops the owner and frees the value.
trap: Expecting GC timing; drop happens deterministically at scope end.

body_md: Assigning a `String` **moves** ownership — old variable becomes invalid. This prevents two owners freeing same heap data. Use-after-move is a compile error, not a crash.
hook: let b = a; kills a — the most shocking line for newcomers.

quiz.explain: Heap types like String move instead of copying.
quiz.q: After `let b = a;` for String, what holds?

takeaway: Assignment of heap values moves ownership.
trap: Using moved value gives `borrow of moved value` error.

body_md: Passing a `String` to a function **moves** it unless you return it. Caller loses ownership. Take `String` only when function should consume the data.
hook: Calling a function can destroy your variable — by design.

quiz.explain: take(s: String) takes ownership, caller cannot reuse s.
quiz.q: What happens when you pass String by value?

takeaway: By-value params consume ownership.
trap: Passing String then reusing it fails; borrow with & instead.

body_md: `.clone()` makes a deep copy of heap data — slow but explicit. Only clone when you truly need two independent owners. Cloning in a loop kills performance.
hook: clone() fixes the compiler error — but seniors flinch when they see it.

quiz.explain: clone duplicates heap data so both bindings are valid.
quiz.q: What does `a.clone()` do for String?

takeaway: Clone duplicates data; use sparingly.
trap: Sprinkling clone to silence moves hides perf costs; prefer borrows.

body_md: Integers, floats, bool, char are `Copy` — assignment duplicates bits, no move. Types with heap data like `String` or `Vec` are never Copy. Custom types opt in with `#[derive(Copy, Clone)]`.
hook: Why do ints survive let b = a but Strings do not?

quiz.explain: i32 is Copy so assignment copies bits.
quiz.q: After `let b = a;` with i32, what happened?

takeaway: Stack-only primitives are Copy; heap types move.
trap: Assuming String is Copy; only Clone works and it is explicit.

body_md: `&s` **borrows** immutably — read without owning. Function gets a reference, caller keeps ownership. Most functions should take `&str` or `&T`, not owned values.
hook: Read data without owning it — the borrow is Rust's superpower.

quiz.explain: Borrowing lets callee read while caller retains ownership.
quiz.q: What happens when you pass `&s`?

takeaway: Borrow with & to read without taking ownership.
trap: Taking String by value when &str suffices forces needless moves.

body_md: Many borrows can coexist: `&T` is **shared**. Ten readers are fine because none can mutate. Data race impossible when mutation is impossible.
hook: Ten people can read the same book — as long as nobody writes in it.

quiz.explain: Multiple immutable borrows can coexist.
quiz.q: How many & borrows can coexist?

takeaway: Unlimited shared borrows are allowed together.
trap: Thinking borrows are exclusive; only &mut is exclusive.

body_md: `&mut s` borrows **exclusively** for mutation. Only one active `&mut` at a time, and no `&` alongside it. Compiler enforces this aliasing rule.
hook: Only one writer allowed — Rust enforces it at compile time.

quiz.explain: Only one live &mut, with no shared borrows alongside.
quiz.q: How many live &mut borrows allowed?

takeaway: Mutable borrows are exclusive by design.
trap: Holding & while creating &mut gives `cannot borrow as mutable` error.

body_md: Borrow checker rule: **either many `&` or one `&mut`, never both**. Violation is compile error, catching data races before they run. NLL ends borrows at last use.
hook: The one borrow rule that kills 90% of data races.

quiz.explain: Either multiple shared or one exclusive, never mixed live.
quiz.q: What is the core borrow rule?

takeaway: Many readers XOR one writer, enforced statically.
trap: Keeping a & alive (e.g. in println later) blocks &mut creation.

body_md: References must never outlive their data. Borrow checker rejects **dangling refs** via lifetimes. `fn dangle() -> &String` cannot compile — owned value drops at return.
hook: This 4-line function is impossible in Rust — and that saves you.

quiz.explain: s drops at function end so returning &s would dangle.
quiz.q: What happens returning &local String?

takeaway: References can never outlive their referent.
trap: Trying to return &String from helper; return owned String instead.

body_md: A **slice** `&[T]` or `&str` is a (pointer, length) view into data you do not own. `&s[0..2]` borrows part of a String. No copy, no ownership change.
hook: Borrow half a string without copying a single byte.

quiz.explain: Slices are fat pointers: address plus length.
quiz.q: What is a slice internally?

takeaway: Slices are lightweight borrowed views.
trap: Slicing mid-UTF8-char panics; slice on char boundaries only.

body_md: Prefer `&str` params over `&String`: they accept String, literals, and slices alike. Deref coercion makes `&String` act as `&str` at call sites automatically.
hook: fn f(s: &String) is almost always wrong — one character fixes it.

quiz.explain: &str is more general; &String derefs to it.
quiz.q: Best param type for read-only text?

takeaway: Take &str for flexible read-only text APIs.
trap: Using &String params rejects literals and slices needlessly.

body_md: **Structs** bundle named fields. Use `struct Name { f: T }`, init with `Name { f }`, access with `.`. `..other` fills remaining fields via struct update syntax.
hook: Classes are gone — this simpler grouping replaces them.

quiz.explain: Structs group named fields with types.
quiz.q: Which groups named fields together?

takeaway: Structs model data with named typed fields.
trap: Forgetting a field in literal errors; use ..base to fill rest.

body_md: Tuple structs `Name(T, U)` and unit structs `Name;` are compact variants. Good for newtypes like `Meters(f64)` that add type safety with zero cost.
hook: A struct with no field names? It is a power move for type safety.

quiz.explain: Newtype wraps one type to prevent mixing (Meters vs Feet).
quiz.q: How do you stop mixing Meters and Feet (both f64)?

takeaway: Newtypes add safety with zero runtime cost.
trap: Forgetting .0 access on tuple structs; fields are positional.

body_md: **Enums** list variants a value can be: `enum Dir { N, S, E, W }`. Variants can hold data: `Some(T)`, `Ok(T)`, `Err(E)`. Use `::` to construct each case.
hook: An enum that carries data inside each option — no nulls needed.

quiz.explain: Enum variants can store associated data.
quiz.q: Can enum variants hold data?

takeaway: Enums encode choices plus their payloads.
trap: Treating enums like ints; use match, not == chains, to unpack.

body_md: `match` must be **exhaustive**: handle every variant or add `_` wildcard. Each arm can bind payloads. Compiler warns if you miss a future variant.
hook: Forget one case and Rust refuses to build — future-you says thanks.

quiz.explain: match requires covering all variants.
quiz.q: What must match cover?

takeaway: Match exhaustively so new variants cannot slip through.
trap: Missing arm gives non-exhaustive pattern error; add _ or variant.

body_md: `if let` handles **one** interesting case, ignoring rest. Shorter than match for single-variant checks. Pair with `let-else` when you need early return on mismatch.
hook: Full match for one case is overkill — this cuts it to two lines.

quiz.explain: if let tests one pattern and binds its payload.
quiz.q: When is if let better than match?

takeaway: Use if let for single-pattern checks.
trap: Using if let when you need exhaustive handling hides missed cases.

body_md: `Option<T>` is `Some(T)` or `None` — Rust's null replacement. No null derefs possible: you must handle None via match, `unwrap_or`, `?`, or combinators before use.
hook: Rust deleted null — and replaced it with something strictly better.

quiz.explain: Option forces explicit None handling at compile time.
quiz.q: How does Option prevent null bugs?

takeaway: Option makes absence explicit and checkable.
trap: Calling unwrap blindly panics on None; prefer unwrap_or or ?.

body_md: Chain Options without nesting: `map` transforms Some, `and_then` chains fallible steps, `unwrap_or` supplies defaults. Keeps happy path flat and readable.
hook: Nested if-Some pyramids collapse into one clean line.

quiz.explain: map/and_then transform and chain Options functionally.
quiz.q: How do you transform Option without manual match?

takeaway: Combinators keep Option pipelines flat.
trap: Using map where and_then needed nests Option<Option<T>>.

body_md: `Result<T, E>` is `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)` for recoverable errors. `match`, `?`, or combinators handle it. Unlike exceptions, error path is visible in the type signature.
hook: Errors as values, not explosions — the signature tells the truth.

quiz.explain: Result encodes success or typed error in the return.
quiz.q: Which type represents success or recoverable error?

takeaway: Result makes errors part of the API contract.
trap: Ignoring Err with let _ hides failures; handle or propagate.

body_md: Methods take `self`, `&self`, or `&mut self` in `impl` blocks. `&self` reads, `&mut self` mutates, `self` consumes. Call with dot: `rect.area()`.
hook: No this, no self confusion — three receivers cover every case.

quiz.explain: &self borrows the instance for reading.
quiz.q: Which receiver reads without consuming?

takeaway: Pick receiver by ownership need: borrow, mutate, or consume.
trap: Using self when &self suffices moves the value unexpectedly.

body_md: Associated functions like `String::new()` have no self — call on type itself. Constructors are just convention: `fn new(...) -> Self`. No `new` keyword needed.
hook: There is no new keyword — yet constructors still exist.

quiz.explain: Associated fns without self act as constructors.
quiz.q: What is `P::new()` with no self param?

takeaway: Constructors are plain associated functions returning Self.
trap: Writing p.new() instead of P::new() confuses instance vs type call.

body_md: `#[derive(Debug)]` auto-implements printing with `{:?}`. Add `Clone`, `PartialEq` similarly. Derives remove boilerplate for common traits instantly.
hook: One line above your struct writes code for you.

quiz.explain: derive generates trait impls like Debug automatically.
quiz.q: How do you auto-implement Debug?

takeaway: Derive common traits instead of hand-writing them.
trap: Forgetting Debug derive then using {:?} fails with formatting error.

body_md: Field init shorthand: `User { name, age }` when variables match field names. Destructuring `let User { name, age } = u;` unpacks similarly. Less repetition, fewer typos.
hook: Stop writing name: name — Rust already knows what you mean.

quiz.explain: Shorthand works when variable names equal field names.
quiz.q: When can you write `User { name, age }`?

takeaway: Use field shorthand to cut boilerplate.
trap: Shadowing a field name then using shorthand binds wrong value.

body_md: Use `let-else` to extract from Option/Result or **diverge** early: `let Some(x) = v else { return; }`. Guarantees x valid after, no nesting, no unwrap.
hook: Unwrap without panicking and without nesting — meet let-else.

quiz.explain: let-else binds on success or diverges (return/break).
quiz.q: How do you extract Option safely with early exit?

takeaway: let-else flattens fallible extraction with early exit.
trap: Else branch must diverge (!); plain fallback value will not compile.
